newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: First post-war Sarajevo buses cross into Serbia.
newsitem.headline: First post-war Sarajevo buses cross into Serbia.

text.p: The first buses from Sarajevo to Belgrade for almost five years crossed the Yugoslav-Bosnian border on Tuesday afternoon after a delay of several hours.
The two Bosnian buses and one owned by the Serbian company Lasta, which was returning from a landmark trip to Sarajevo on Monday, later rolled into Belgrade's main bus terminal.

Some 80 passengers disembarked under the glare of strobe lights of television crews covering their arrival which, as one Sarajevan said, "symbolized the new post-Dayton era in the region -- no more killing and desire for rapprochement."
Many of the passengers spoke of this simple act as a huge step, unimaginable only one year ago when the Bosnian war was still in progress.
"The last time I was here in the Spring of 1994, I was afraid to enter the city. Now I am not," Vanja Ilic, a reporter from the Sarajevo daily newspaper Dnevni Avaz told Reuters.
The restoration of bus links was a concrete result of recently forged diplomatic relations between Sarajevo and Belgrade, which has snubbed its former Bosnian Serb proteges.

Yugoslavia and Bosnia agreed in Paris earlier this month to establish full diplomatic relations and increase trade and transport, establish a customs union and permit visa-free travel between the two countries.
The deal was criticized by the Bosnian Serb authorities who besieged Sarajevo for 43 months, killing more than 10,000 people and wounding another 50,000.

For some Serbs from Yugoslavia who visited Sarajevo on Monday for the first time since the war broke out in April 1992 and had never seen the full extent of the devastation meted out by their ethnic kin, the journey had a sobering effect.

"All the destruction we have seen so far (on Serbian state Television) isn't even one-sixth of what had really happened there. You feel horrible, although you had nothing to do with it," a reporter from Serbian state media said, speaking on condition of anonimity.
"Sarajevans welcomed us heartily but the barriers are there. It will never be the way it was," he said referring to the firm bonds the two cities once had.
Some said they were touched by a gesture by their hosts, who had Sarajevo musicians play traditional Serbian music at a ceremonial dinner for the visitors on Monday night.
Independent Belgrade Television BK reported earlier that two buses owned by the Sarajevo company Centrotrans were held up at the border because they lacked proper documents to cross.
"The Yugoslav police did not let us go for five to six hours, demanding we pay 60 German marks ($40) for tourist visas," Adi Sarajlic, a journalist from Sarajevo radio Zid said.
"Then they said military conscripts could not enter the country, only women and children. The problem was resolved only after telephone calls to various ministries in Sarajevo and Belgrade," he said.
The first bus from Belgrade since the Bosnian war broke out in 1992 arrived in Sarajevo on Monday.

The bus, carrying 39 Serbian journalists and businessmen, was greeted with applause from waiting dignitaries as Bosnian federation Vice-President Ejup Ganic described the new service as a decisive step towards normalization of bilateral relations and a clear message to those opposed to the process.
The Bosnian Serbs have so far resisted international pressure to join Bosnia's governing bodies under the terms of the Dayton peace accord.
"Surprisingly the journey through the Bosnian Serb republic was trouble-free. There were some astonished faces and an occasional (traditional Serb) three-finger salute," Ilic said.
The Belgrade transport company Lasta and Sarajevo's Centrotrans signed a contract to enable their buses to shuttle between the cities on a daily basis from Wednesday.

Centrotrans manager Muhamed Saciragic said the company was on the verge of striking a deal with Yugoslav partners on setting up 18 more bus lines with other Serbian cities, some of them expected to be running by mid-November.
